name: OSI SYSTEMS

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That I have replaced a conservative base with a generous one and then called the result fair. The strongest form: the engine's three-year mean is doing exactly what its own docstring says it is for — damping working-capital lumpiness — and I have overridden it toward the single most favourable year in the window on the argument that the unfavourable year was special. But fiscal 2024 was not special: OSI Systems' business model IS large turnkey Security contracts with multi-year receivable cycles, the book-to-bill is 1.4 and backlog just jumped 11% in a quarter, so another build year is not a tail risk, it is the predictable consequence of the bookings the bull case is celebrating. On that reading the mean is the honest number and the engine's +41.8% required growth, while high, is pointing at something real: an enterprise value of $4.0bn against a business that has generated $258M of cumulative free cash flow across three years, i.e. about $86M a year, is a 2.1% free-cash-flow yield. Separately, my $190M base is not corroborated by any company-guided cash-flow figure — OSI Systems guides revenue and EPS, not free cash flow — so unlike the HOG and JBI cases I have no filed number to check it against.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Fiscal 2027 full-year operating cash flow against the $275.9M of fiscal 2026, and specifically the direction of accounts receivable. If the record backlog is funded by a receivable build, operating cash flow falls back toward the $97.6M of fiscal 2025 even as EPS rises, and my $190M base is wrong by a third. The second and cheaper test is the quarterly sequence: the first quarter delivered $37.1M of operating cash flow, so a full year needs the remaining three quarters to average roughly $50M. The third is whether capitalised software development costs keep rising from the $5.6M quarterly rate, since that is capital spending the free-cash-flow definition on this brief does not charge.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Partly, and it is genuinely two-sided, which is what keeps this at no_edge. For my base: first-quarter operating cash flow more than doubled year over year to $37.1M, which is an annualised run rate well above the $74.1M the engine uses and consistent with my range rather than with the mean. Against my base: the quarter is seasonally the weakest for this filer and $37.1M annualised is about $148M, which sits BELOW my $190M midpoint, so the one clean forward data point I have argues the lower half of my range. The devil's advocate therefore wins on the magnitude without reversing the direction — the engine's base is demonstrably too low, but my correction is probably too generous, and the honest reading is nearer $160M than $215M. At $160M and +10% the equity is worth $126 against $208, which would make the name rich rather than fair. That is why I record no_edge and the range rather than a verdict: the sign of the answer moves with a base I cannot pin down, and across the defensible band the fair value spans roughly $113 to $238 against a $208 price.
devils_advocate.unresolved: The direction of working capital in fiscal 2027, which is the single input that decides this name and which no filing can yet tell me — the first quarter is one observation and the seasonally weakest. I also could not find any company-guided free-cash-flow or operating-cash-flow figure to anchor the base against, so my $190M is a construction rather than a reconciliation, which is a materially weaker position than on the names where management publishes a cash-flow guide. And I did not read the first-quarter earnings call, where the receivable question would have been put to management directly.

what_changed: The fiscal 2027 first-quarter 10-Q and earnings release were both filed 2026-10-29, the day before this pass, and the engine's extract predates them — its balance sheet is the 2026-06-30 10-K. The new quarter is materially better than the base the model is using: operating cash flow of $37.1M against $17.1M a year earlier, more than doubling, on capital expenditure of $7.7M. Revenue $403.5M (+5%), GAAP EPS +28%, non-GAAP EPS +17%, book-to-bill 1.4, backlog a record $2.1bn (from $1.9bn three months earlier), and fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance raised to $11.28-$11.64 from $11.13-$11.49 while revenue guidance was reaffirmed at $1.875-1.930bn. The company repurchased 305,559 shares in the quarter — roughly 1.9% of the shares outstanding in three months — with 773,172 remaining under authorisation after the board added 1 million shares in August 2026. Also relevant and new to me from the fiscal 2026 10-K: management attributes the fiscal 2026 cash-flow surge explicitly to 'favorable changes in net working capital, largely from lower accounts receivable, an increase in deferred revenue and other liabilities, as well as higher net income', and names 'collections on large Security projects' as the driver — which identifies the three-year cash-flow series as one working-capital cycle rather than a trend.
consensus_case: At $208.17 against fiscal 2027 non-GAAP earnings per share guidance of $11.28-$11.64, OSI Systems trades on about 18.2x forward earnings — and the market is paying that for visibility rather than for growth. The first quarter of fiscal 2027, reported 2026-10-29, was a record on both lines: revenue $403.5M (+5%), GAAP diluted EPS $1.51 (+28%), non-GAAP $1.66 (+17%), a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4 and backlog at a record $2.1bn against $1.9bn at June 30 — an 11% increase in one quarter. Management reaffirmed revenue guidance and RAISED non-GAAP EPS guidance. The gap between GAAP and non-GAAP EPS is only $0.15, so this is not an adjusted-earnings story. Against that, three things justify restraint rather than enthusiasm: revenue growth is guided at only 5.0-8.1%, the Healthcare division is shrinking, and the Security division is described as delivering 'despite continued geopolitical headwinds'. A market asking roughly 18x for a business compounding earnings at 9-12.5% with two years of backlog is making a reasonable, unexciting judgment. The engine's claim that this is among the most EXPENSIVE 10% of 125 Information Technology names, requiring +41.8% cash-flow growth, is not what the market is doing.
base_case_rationale: I underwrite +10% real FCFF growth off an overridden through-cycle base of $190M rather than the engine's $74.1M. The base first, because it is the whole story. The engine's figure is the mean of free cash flow of $245.3M, $73.8M and -$109.6M (newest first), and I verified all three against the 10-K cash flow statement: operating cash flow was -$87,501k in fiscal 2024, $97,592k in fiscal 2025 and $275,904k in fiscal 2026, against property-and-equipment capex of $22.1M, $23.8M and about $30.6M. That series is not a cycle in the business, it is a single working-capital wave on large turnkey Security contracts — receivables built through fiscal 2024 and were collected through fiscal 2026 — so averaging the build year against the collection year understates normal generation badly. The newest year alone is 3.3x the mean. Building it from economics instead: fiscal 2027 guidance implies about $182M of non-GAAP net income (EPS midpoint $11.46 on roughly 15.9M shares), add back depreciation and amortisation, deduct true capital expenditure of about $50M (the $30.6M of property and equipment PLUS roughly $20M a year of capitalised software development the extractor omits — $5.6M in the first quarter alone), and charge the working-capital growth that a 1.4 book-to-bill on turnkey contracts genuinely consumes. That lands between $160M on a conservative through-cycle charge and $215M on an EBITDA-less-capex-less-tax construction; $190M is the midpoint. On the growth rate, +10% sits at the middle of the guided 9.0-12.5% non-GAAP EPS growth and above the guided 5.0-8.1% revenue growth, which is the right shape for a business whose backlog is growing faster than its revenue — but I hold it below the EPS figure because free cash flow has to fund the receivable build that record bookings create, and fiscal 2024 is the evidence that this can swallow a year's cash entirely.
key_risks: The engine's $74.1M FCFF base is the mean of one working-capital wave (operating cash flow -$87.5M, +$97.6M, +$275.9M across fiscal 2024-26 on large Security project collections), and the whole -83.0% gap and 10th-percentile rank follow from it — but my $190M correction is itself uncorroborated by any guided cash-flow figure
A 1.4 book-to-bill and an 11% quarterly backlog increase are precisely what caused the fiscal 2024 receivable build; record bookings on turnkey contracts consume cash before they produce it
Capitalised software development costs of $5.6M in the quarter (~$20M a year) are capital spending the brief's free-cash-flow definition does not charge, so the base is overstated by that much
Healthcare division revenue is declining and the Security division faces 'continued geopolitical headwinds' on international order conversion
Revenue growth is guided at only 5.0-8.1%, so the 9.0-12.5% EPS growth depends on margin expansion and buybacks rather than volume
Stock compensation is 42% of the engine's base (about $31M a year, ~16% of my corrected base), though the share count is shrinking fast enough to cover it
watch_for: Fiscal 2027 full-year operating cash flow against fiscal 2026's $275.9M, and specifically the direction of accounts receivable — the single number that decides the base
The quarterly cash-flow sequence: a full year consistent with my $190M base needs the remaining three quarters to average roughly $50M against the first quarter's $37.1M
Whether capitalised software development costs keep rising from the $5.6M quarterly rate
Backlog conversion at stable gross margin, and whether the Optoelectronics mix stabilisation and service-revenue growth management flagged actually arrive
Continued buyback at the first quarter's pace — 305,559 shares, about 1.9% of the company in three months, with 773,172 remaining authorised
